lead: Real gases do not obey PV = RT, especially near the critical point and at high pressure. The compressibility factor Z = PV/RT measures the departure. Instead of a separate table for every gas, generalized correlations use reduced temperature and pressure, and the acentric factor, to give Z from one chart or one equation. Chemical engineers use them for quick volume estimates, pipeline sizing and checking equations of state.
prereq: You need: equations of state for critical constants and cubic equations, and the ideal gas law.

blocks.text: For one mole, an ideal gas obeys PV = RT. Define the compressibility factor Z = PV/RT. Here P is pressure, V is molar volume, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. Z is dimensionless. An ideal gas has Z = 1 at every T and P. A real gas has Z below or above 1.

Z below 1 means attractive forces dominate, so the volume is smaller than ideal. Z above 1 means molecular size and repulsion dominate, so the volume is larger than ideal. At very low pressure every gas approaches Z = 1. Near the critical point Z can be far from 1. Z is a function of T and P for each gas, not a constant.

blocks.where: V is molar volume, Z is the compressibility factor, R is the gas constant, T is absolute temperature, and P is pressure.

items: Reduced temperature: T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>, where T<sub>c</sub> is the critical temperature.
Reduced pressure: P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub>, where P<sub>c</sub> is the critical pressure.
Reduced volume: V<sub>r</sub> = V/V<sub>c</sub>, where V<sub>c</sub> is the critical molar volume.
T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and V<sub>r</sub> are dimensionless.

sections.h3: Corresponding states and the acentric factor

blocks.text: The principle of corresponding states says that fluids at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> have approximately the same Z. This is why one generalized compressibility chart can serve many gases. It is a two-parameter correlation: T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub> fix the reduced coordinates.

Simple spherical molecules (argon, krypton, methane) follow this rule well. Polar and long molecules need a third parameter, the Pitzer acentric factor ω = −1.0 − log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup>) at T<sub>r</sub> = 0.7. For simple fluids P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 0.1 there, so ω = 0; for n-butane ω = 0.200. The three-parameter correlation adds a correction term proportional to ω.

blocks.where: Z⁰ is the simple-fluid compressibility factor, Z¹ is its correction, and ω is the Pitzer acentric factor; both Z⁰ and Z¹ depend on T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this the generalized compressibility factor correlation. For nonpolar gases it is accurate enough for quick design checks. For strongly polar or associating gases, use an equation of state with better mixing rules.

sections.h3: Reading a chart and using generalized equations

items: Look up T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub> for the gas.
Compute T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub>.
Find the curve for T<sub>r</sub> and move to the value P<sub>r</sub> on the horizontal axis.
Read Z from the vertical axis.
Compute V = ZRT/P, keeping R consistent with the pressure and volume units.

blocks.text: A generalized equation of state is written in Tr, Pr and ω, so it returns Z for any gas from three tabulated constants. The simplest is the Pitzer virial correlation, the truncated virial equation with B made generalized:

blocks.where: B⁰ and B¹ are dimensionless functions of T<sub>r</sub> only; the group (B⁰ + ωB¹) equals BP<sub>c</sub>/RT<sub>c</sub>.

blocks.text: Z is then linear in pressure, so the correlation holds only where the real isotherm is nearly straight: low to moderate Pr (roughly Vr ≥ 2, or Pr below about 1 at Tr = 1.2). At higher pressure use the chart or a generalized cubic. Any cubic from the cubic table can be put in reduced form with β = ΩPr/Tr and q = Ψα(Tr)/(ΩTr), and solved by repeated substitution from Z = 1:
Z = 1 + β − qβ(Z − β)/[(Z + εβ)(Z + σβ)]
blocks.where: β and q are dimensionless; ε and σ are the same pure numbers as in the generic cubic.

blocks.text: T<sub>pc</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>T<sub>c,i</sub>,  P<sub>pc</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>P<sub>c,i</sub>  (Kay's rule)
blocks.where: y<sub>i</sub> is the mole fraction and T<sub>c,i</sub>, P<sub>c,i</sub> are the component critical constants; T<sub>pc</sub> and P<sub>pc</sub> are pseudo-critical values used in place of T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub>. Kay's rule is rough when the components differ much in size or polarity (natural gas with CO<sub>2</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>S); use a cubic with mixing rules there.

figure.caption: Z against reduced pressure at T<sub>r</sub> = 1.2 for ω = 0.20, from the generalized Peng–Robinson equation (solid) and the Pitzer virial correlation (dashed). They agree at low P<sub>r</sub>: worked example 2 (n-butane, P<sub>r</sub> = 0.659) gives 0.879 and 0.858. Beyond P<sub>r</sub> ≈ 1 the straight virial line drifts away, and only the chart or the cubic gives example 1's Z = 0.61 at P<sub>r</sub> = 2.

spec.aria: Compressibility factor from 0.4 to 1.1 against reduced pressure from 0 to 3 at reduced temperature 1.2. A dotted line at Z equals 1 marks the ideal gas. The solid Peng-Robinson curve falls from 1 to about 0.58 near Pr 2.5 and turns up slightly; the dashed Pitzer virial straight line follows it at low pressure and drifts away from it after Pr 1. Points mark n-butane at Pr 0.659 with Z 0.879 and 0.858, and example 1 at Pr 2 with Z 0.61.

examples.question: A gas has T<sub>c</sub> = 300 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 50 bar and ω = 0.20. At T = 360 K and P = 100 bar its generalized chart (Z⁰ + ωZ¹) gives Z = 0.61. Find T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and the molar volume, using R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K).
steps: P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub> = 100 bar / 50 bar = 2.00. These two numbers, not T and P, are what you look up on the chart.

Cross-check: the generalized Peng–Robinson equation at T<sub>r</sub> = 1.2, P<sub>r</sub> = 2.0, ω = 0.20 gives Z = 0.609, the same to chart accuracy. The Pitzer virial line would give 0.633, already drifting (see the figure).
examples.answer: T<sub>r</sub> = 1.20, P<sub>r</sub> = 2.00 and V = 0.183 L/mol, about 39 % less than the ideal-gas 0.299 L/mol.
examples.check:
R = 0.08314
T = 360.0
P = 100.0
Tc = 300.0
Pc = 50.0
Z = 0.65
Tr = T / Tc
Pr = P / Pc
V = Z * R * T / P
print(round(Tr, 3))
print(round(Pr, 3))
print(round(V, 3))

examples.question: Estimate the molar volume of n-butane at 510 K and 25 bar (T<sub>c</sub> = 425.1 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 37.96 bar, ω = 0.200) by (a) the ideal gas law, (b) the Pitzer virial correlation and (c) the generalized Peng–Robinson equation. Use R = 83.14 cm³·bar/(mol·K).
steps: P<sub>r</sub> = 0.66 is inside the Pitzer range, so (b) and (c) agree within 2.5 %; the ideal gas is 14 to 17 % high.
examples.answer: Ideal 1696 cm³/mol; Pitzer virial Z = 0.879, V = 1491 cm³/mol; Peng–Robinson Z = 0.858, V = 1455 cm³/mol.

traps: Using T and P directly on the chart without first computing T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>.
Assuming Z = 1 at high pressure because the gas is called permanent; high pressure usually increases deviation from ideal behaviour.
Mixing units: T must be absolute, P and P<sub>c</sub> must use the same unit, and R must match the chosen pressure and volume units.
Treating a chart reading as exact; generalized charts are approximate, so do not report more digits than the chart supports.
Using the two-parameter chart for a polar gas when the acentric factor or a better equation of state is needed.

quiz.q: Define the compressibility factor Z and state its value for an ideal gas.
quiz.a: Z = PV/RT, where P is pressure, V is molar volume, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. For an ideal gas Z = 1.

quiz.q: Why do reduced temperature and reduced pressure let one chart serve many gases?
quiz.a: The principle of corresponding states says that fluids at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> have approximately the same Z. Critical constants scale out the differences between gases.

quiz.q: A gas has T<sub>c</sub> = 200 K and P<sub>c</sub> = 40 bar. At T = 400 K and P = 20 bar, a chart gives Z = 0.90. Find T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and V using R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Two gases have the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> but different Z. What third parameter improves the correlation, and why can it still fail for polar gases?
quiz.a: The Pitzer acentric factor ω, through Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹ (or B⁰ + ωB¹). It measures how far the vapour-pressure curve departs from that of a simple fluid. Strongly polar or hydrogen-bonding gases can still deviate, because one shape parameter cannot describe directional forces.

quiz.q: What does Z < 1 mean physically for a real gas?
quiz.a: The gas volume is smaller than the ideal-gas volume at the same T and P. Attractive forces dominate over size and repulsion effects.

quiz.q: For the gas of worked example 1 (Z = 0.61 at 360 K and 100 bar), find the ideal-gas volume and the percent by which it exceeds the real volume.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators use generalized correlations for quick checks and cubic equations of state for final design. The acentric factor appears in Pitzer correlations and in mixing rules for reservoir fluids. Search for Pitzer correlation, Lee-Kesler tables, and corresponding states for mixtures.
